What an intense game! When they said 'horror experience' they did not lie! Imagine yourself waking up one day and someone delivered a phone to you, and not any normal phone, it is a missing person's phone. The game starts off with you having Anna's phone, you played a video of her saying weird stuff and not to find her, however, when you go through her messages and dig deeper into her personal life, you will discover many things. Would you trust her boyfriend who seems to be worried or someone who she chatted with online? You will make this choice and end up with one of the four possible endings of this game. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997884297

The gameplay is all about texting, reading text messages, going to social media, solve some puzzles to find phone numbers, passwords or people to contact. It is a fun deep game and has lots of jumpscares! I gasped so many times and couldn't stop playing the game until I've finished it, and yes, that took me 9 hours to finish with little breaks in between. 

I was torn between the answers, yes you are limited with the answers they provided you but sometimes you wish to side with someone, the next moment you hear something from the other character which will make you suspect the first one. I ended up suspecting everyone including myself. 
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997329266

The actors were mediocre, none of them showed the supposed emotion the person would in such a situation, the facial expression wasn't the best especially Anna and Taylor. However the writing of the game and how the story flows is really good, I didn't expect that twist.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=1997329744

Pros:
+Well-written story.
+Jumpscares.
+Around 8 hours of gameplay.
+Multiple endings.
+High replay value. 
+Good puzzles.
+Steam achievements.

Cons:
-The characters are real people with mediocre acting.
-No hinting system.

I highly recommend this game, you can play it with your friend for a spooky weekend. I enjoyed it so much and still working on the rest of the achievements.

[b]Playing status:[/b] 100% achievement, 4x + playthroughs
[b]Grindy Achievement(s):[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement(s):[/b] Yes (16 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement(s):[/b] No.

[h1]Intro[/h1]
You found a lost phone. Inside, you find someone asking for help. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] puts you in the shoe of a stranger who is trying to find the owner of a lost phone. Will you succeed or will you fail?

[b]Pros:[/b]
- 4 endings with slight story branches
- New game plus let you play the game with faster chat speed

[b]Cons:[/b]
- No manual save and extra save slot to make it easier to unlock all endings
- Not suitable for people who have issues with flashing lights

[b]Specs[/b]
Intel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to read a visual novel that was told through phone and chats, feel free to buy this game at a sale.[/i]

[hr][/hr]
[h1]In-Depth Review[/h1]

[h3]Visuals[/h3]
As a game that is played out on a smartphone, the game does well to simulate the phone-like interface. It has a photo app, a contact book, a chat app - anything that you'll expect from a smartphone. Its functionality is limited tough. There is no option to switch between tabs nor a scroll bar on the right side of the screen to scroll the page faster.

[h3]Story[/h3]
The story is played out from series of chats. Expect a lot of typos and shortened words due to the informal context. This brings forth the characters' personality though, especially since everyone has a unique texting style from each other. Some information can also be retrieved by watching videos and receiving phone calls, although their voice is not expressive enough - it feels dragged out on purpose to make it easier for non-native English speakers to listen to. It does make them easier to hear, but it also kills their expression in the process.

Interface aside, the presentation helps with the storytelling. The glitchy screen and a few jumpscares help to set the mysterious vibe, while the surprising phone calls freak me out sometimes. It got toned down as you play the game, focusing more on the mysterious element. The writing was done well in regards to what's happening and sometimes, you will have several options to choose from. Despite giving the same outcome, the conversation will play out differently based on which option that you choose. However, some sentences are not flowing smoothly after choosing a certain option, giving you the impression that you chose the wrong one.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225479 

[h3]The Game[/h3]
[b]Gameplay[/b]
The gameplay is focused on chatting with people and exploring everything that is inside the phone that you used. As I said before, sometimes you will have to choose between several options to proceed. Some of them will affect the endings, some are not. Some old chat and photos will also be encrypted, allowing you to play a minigame to restore their state, which takes form in arranging photos or word. It's quite easy to finish although some words might be difficult to arrange sometimes.

Hints are usually provided whenever you are stuck. You can ask people to figure out what you are supposed to do and they will gladly help you out. However, I got stuck twice with no idea to proceed. Although one is expected since I never do well with puzzles that have vague rules, another feels like they don't give enough hints to solve.

[b]Length and Difficulty[/b]
I finished the game in ~4h, and proceed to replay the game several times to get all achievements. The new game+ helps a lot by providing a faster chat speed, allowing you to finish the game faster. However, you still need to wait for the voice-over near the ending to finish, and they talk very slowly. It was tiring to wait for them to finish talking and playing the game several times to unlock all four endings become not fun anymore. I wish there is an option to fast-forward the game at this point.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2466225684 

[b]Problems[/b]
Although the game has a phone-like interface, some quality of life features are missing, notably the option to switch tabs in the browser (or the option to keep existing tab), and the feature to start a video from a certain timestamp. There were also some occasions when I had to type some forms and I couldn't use the tab button in my keyboard to switch between text boxes. Lastly, there are some flashing lights near the ending - people who have issues with it might want to stay out of the game.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
For a visual novel game, it still can be enjoyed with people who don't like to read a wall of text. You might need to read a lot, but they are mostly in the form of short chats which shouldn't take long to finish. The story picks up an interesting topic that is enhanced with its mysterious vibe, and although the story feels weak at times, it still proves to be an enjoyable read.

review_text_raw:
When you are a mature person and your childhood and carefree days are already over, you have kinda stressful job, you don't feel like playing hard games, or games where you have to concentrate a lot. Sometimes, you just want to come over to your place. make yourself a cup of tea and just relax on comfortable chair and just enjoy some kinda easy game. Preferably, with a mouse only controls.

But to be honest, you need to be ready that games will be strange, or better call them weird or maybe even creepy in some kinda way, cause variety of the titles, that can be played with mouse only is pretty limited and you should expect only chinese visual novels, or some nonsense clickers, or easy tower defense games, or some puzzle logic games.

Or it can be a game like Simulacra. I am not even sure how to call this genre, but what I really do know for sure - this game is completely stupid :) But, in a good funny way. They call it a simulation game, which is kinda fair, but doesn't cover the whole idea of this game. 

So, you start the game playing as not a man, not a woman, just whoever the hell you are, sex is not specified in this game. You found a smartphone and this is where the whole stupid part is about to start. I mean like, imagine you are that person who found a phone, okay? What you gonna do? For me it's completely obvious and easy - if phone is unlockable, you simply need to find someone with a name Mom, Dad, Sister, Boyfriend, Dog in a contact list, call one of them and let them know that you found this device and return it as soon as possible. In case phone is locked, you just need to go to the police station and give it to them for the further actions. Easy as that, don't you think so? But not for our protagonist! Instead all of this, he/she decides to play around with this phone and read messages/mail, check web history, tinder-alike app - I mean like literally everything what you don't have to do, when you find someone's phone, cause this is simply embarassing. For the whole game I had that feeling that I was playing as a retard, who had no job, no personal life, no entertainment sources, literally nothing, so that phone was a greatest relief ever. 

But, on the other hand, if that person wouldn't be that miserable and pathetic and wouldn't check that messages and videos on the camera roll - he wouldn't realize that phones belonged to someone who was desperately crying for help, stucked in some kinda danger. The more you click on that stupid phone the more stranger and uglier everything becomes, and you have to solve some kinda puzzles. All these puzzle things are more like "choose the right answer" in dialogues with a random people, talking about phone's owner, which is also a random person for you lol, which you shouldn't care about at all and all these combinations of answers lead you to different endings. Plus you have to recreate some corrupted messages, by putting words in the right order and renew corrupted photos by clicking on image pieces at the right order. Time to time, you will see ugly screamers on the phone, whose aim is to scarry you and like, to be honest, this one of the most ridiculous things in this game, cause I was laughing all the time when that was appearing on the screen, so I can't say that this game is a horror experience, it's more "wannabe horror game" , trying to be mysterious and creepy all the way ends up with a pretty shallow and a bit boring idea.

However, I can recommend this game. It brings you some fresh new experience and can be funny a little bit plus you can relax after a busy stressful day by just clicking on the dialogue options and solving pretty easy puzzles trying to figure out what the hell is going on there. 

So, to sum everything up!
You should grab this game if you: 

+ Feel like playing some easy game, where is no need for high concentration
+ Are a Black Mirror TV show fan and like all this paranoic idea about how it can be bad somewhere in the future for us with all these high-tech devices
+ Don't agree with me, that carrying a phone to the police station would be the best idea in this situation :)
+ Just looking for a new experience

Avoid this game if you:

- Don't like illogical games, with a stupid protagonist who has no idea what the hell is he doing 
- Have no desire to try something new and unusual

Enjoy!

review_text_raw:
If you're only just now hearing about Simulacra because it got a sequel, don't feel bad... you're not alone. Somehow this sci-fi horror simulation game ended up flying under the radar of a lot of people until recently. It comes from Kaigan Games, the creators of Sarah Is Missing; a title unavailable on Steam, but is playable for free over on Itch.io. It's a very similar predecessor to Simulacra, and perhaps it helped to serve as an unrefined beta for this more solid-feeling experience.

To say much about the story is to give away the entire game, so to give a very brief synopsis... you found a phone on your doorstep. Opening and accessing its apps leads you to discover that it was previously owned by a girl named Anna. After some digging around in the contents of the device and chatting with her boyfriend and best friend, you realize that Anna has gone missing, and she has been missing for some time. You'll have to recover data, browse photos and videos, and consult with others who were in touch with Anna before her disappearance in order to try and figure out what happened to her, and if you're capable of finding her and saving her life.

The entire game centers around Anna's phone; there's never a time where you will not be using it. The developers have done an outstanding job with creating an entire, believable world within the device; it's fabulously easy to slip into the realm of Simulacra and lose hours of time just checking out all of the dating profiles, work e-mails, and off-beat articles that were added to make the game just that much more realistic. There are several of these websites and news articles to read through, handfuls of in-depth e-mails, tons of selfies of Anna that show off her life and interests, and apps that simulate ones that most of us have installed on our own phones. Of course, a lot of these things are essential components to solving little detective-style puzzles, but there's also a good portion that is just there for entertainment. The game feels like an expansive ARG (alternate reality game), and if one were to play this title on an actual mobile device then the immersion would be surreal.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now.

Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards.

There are very few areas here that need any work, but the voice acting is one of them. A lot of the voice-overs, especially for Anna's boyfriend, are just embarrassingly cringe-worthy. The acting seen in many of the videos is also pretty bad, but not as bad as the voice work. Those are the only real complaints here, and they're honestly just nitpicky as they can be overlooked with ease. The game's interface is user-friendly, there's a great speed up option unlocked after beating the story once so that players can quickly get to the other four endings (as there are five) and explore different dialogue options, and there's enough small little horror elements to keep the gameplay tense throughout the first playthrough. Overall, it's one of the best casual, story-based sci-fi horror experiences out there right now. Simulacra is one of those rare gems that manages to slip under the radar of most people; despite being out for almost three years and having over 1,000 reviews on Steam. It's the perfect blend of technology-based sci-fi and subtle horror, in the same vein of TV shows like Black Mirror and Dark Net. While its premise might sound cheesy, this title has some of the most immersive content that I've ever personally witnessed in the thousands of games that I've played. It borders on being an ARG, as there is an incredible level of attention to detail within every app, website, and chat that you'll delve into. Though an initial playthrough only takes about four hours, that time will be sucked away and you'll be left wondering how the hell it got so late, so fast. You'll also be left craving more, so definitely check out Sarah Is Missing and Simulacra 2 afterwards. review_text_raw:
[b]Last time I pick up a random phone.[/b]

One day, you find a phone just sitting on your doorstep. Like anybody else, you decide to snoop through the phone either to figure out who the owner is so you can return it or just because you can. However, this turns into a much more complicated situation. The first tip off is that while you are blocked by a lock screen, the phone glitches so you can get into it. I don’t know about anybody else, but I wouldn’t have looked through it after that. Anyway, you soon find out that the phone’s owner is Anna and she has recently gone missing. Thus, you decide to look through her phone activity and talk to her friends and acquaintances in an attempt to find her before it’s too late.

There are some puzzles here with the most frequent puzzle you’ll come across involves unscrambling text messages and photos. For texts, you’ll have to order the words in the right order. Photos are more complicated as you’re given several fragments to piece together, but you can’t have any part that is glitched. So you’ll have to figure out which order will allow all glitched out parts to be replaced with the picture. The other puzzle you’ll come across involve you gathering information through either the sites Anna frequented or through her friends. The only problem I had was that some messages had more than one way that it could make sense and that there is an instance where you’re expected to remember certain facts since you can’t go and look for the information.

The acting is average, with Anna’s actress being the stand out, with hilariously bad parts (aka all of Greg’s voice lines) sprinkled in. Voice acting mainly comes through Anna’s vlogs, audio text messages, and phone calls. What doesn’t exactly make sense are the phone calls. At certain points in the story, you’ll get a phone call from one of the characters and you’ll have to answer it (or they’ll keep calling/story won’t continue). Of course, you can’t answer back and when that character asks why you don’t talk back, the excuse is that you can’t make out what they’re saying (despite you being able to hear them fine). I’d rather have the excuse either be that you guess the mic got broken before you found it (which can also imply that whatever is making the phone glitch is causing the mic to stop working) or it auto sends them to voicemail. [spoiler]It doesn’t make sense even more when a police officer actually calls you but assume he’s leaving a voicemail despite not hearing “leave a message after the beep”.[/spoiler]

[spoiler]Also, I just couldn’t help but laugh at the look she gives Taylor in the ending where both of them live.[/spoiler]

Simulacra has four endings each with their own requirements. While you can’t jump to a specific section of the game, you’ll be able to speed things up on your next playthroughs through Begin+. It won’t take long to build up the requirements you need, but the last sequence plays at the same speed.

While Simulacra isn’t perfect, it’s still worth it to experience it yourself, whether it be on PC or on your phone to get the maximum immersion you can. I did find the phone aspect convincing for the most part, didn’t mind that glitches were used to freak you out (though others might not like it), and liked how they filled in the empty space with a room with ambient noises chiming in. There are even some subtle moments here, like the phone’s background changing. The only thing that really messes with immersion is some of the voice acting.

review_text_raw:
Although this hasn't dethroned The Black Watchmen for the title of my favorite alternate reality game, SIMULACRA is worth a play for anyone who's looking for something spooky, casual, immersive, and a bit of a brainteaser. The price point can't be beat, though I will say that I suspect that playing the appstore version on your phone would probably be more immersive than playing it over Steam.

The story starts with you finding a phone belonging to an attractive girl named Anna. You're allowed to navigate through her email account, her texts, her pics/vids, and various social media accounts, and you quickly figure out that something is seriously amiss. As you contact her friends, ex-boyfriend and other acquaintances you understand that your role as the player is to do quite a lot of snooping and social engineering to uncover whatever happened to Anna. Your choices are saved throughtout the play and shape the ultimate outcome of the story - I believe there are 4 different endings.

You do need to play it a bit smart; at points you will need to obtain access to accounts and people that are not obvious, which may require you to dig deeper into photos and media feeds to discover the information you need. I did not find any of the 'puzzles' overly difficult, but a few did give me some pause while I dug up the information needed to continue.

There is both live acting and voice acting throughout the game, so you definitely need your sound on to play. Some of the voice acting seems very forced (and some voice actors in particular are rather annoying to listen to) but the pics and vids felt real enough and the chats you have with other characters did a good job of giving each one a solid personality.

There is a horror element to the story, but I did not see any overt gore or violence from my own playthrough. There is something of a jumpscare towards the end, but nothing too bad. Lots of Exorcist style demon-grumbling, static, spooky messages and so on to set the mood as you go.

So overall, for the price, it's a worthwhile buy if this type of game appeals to you.

After the success of [b]Sara Is Missing[/b], it was obvious [i]Kaigan Games[/i] would continue in the same vein of development. Truth is, before [b]Sara is Missing[/b], there was [b]Finding Home[/b], an indie game also simulating a smartphone experience. Seems the studio entire direction is surrounded by this peculiar genre, one that connects players into a stylized voyeur adventure never seen before.

In [b]SIMULACRA[/b] players gain access to a smartphone belonging to a young woman named Anna. She’s just like any other girl in her early 20’s, working and having a good time with her friends online and offline. All seems perfectly fine, except Anna went missing and she left a strange, bizarre video, as her last registered action.

The overall story is embedded within Anna’s online actions, and each new lead will reveal parts of her past, with phone backups and confessions from her friends. Dialogues are pretty realistic and interesting, making the overall experience more pleasant. There’s no drama, but it’s still somehow intense with a touch of horror and matching jump scares.

Players will explore Anna’s inner secrets and sneak peek into her life, as well as in her problems. Through smartphone apps, such as email, chats, and even the equivalent of Twitter and Tinder, we’ll meet her acquaintances and find clues that may lead to Anna’s whereabouts. While browsing text and pictures, we can restore them by either forming a phrase out of loose words, and building an image by restoring little pieces at a time.

Finding Anna is as much part of the story, as create a connection with other persons of interest through social media. You’ll have to find clues and discover ways to connect with others, to collect new information. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] allows you to open up, or, in some cases, keep pretending to be Anna, which may open up new dialogue options and information.

There’s a certain acquired taste when going through someone else’s life, and the game clearly explores that with decency, but still waving a round or two of peculiar situations and encounters. Some internet references and expressions can be found all over the place, adding a certain style and characterization of realism into that social media life.

It’s one of those experiences, where you’ll forget you’re in the game. As soon as the clues start rolling down and the story involving, it’s a fantastic journey. Gathering clues and finding the direction to go was always relatively easy, and I never found myself stuck or without an idea of where to go. The game also contains a section with the objectives, which will help out in most scenarios if needed.

The visual presentation is accurate and suiting. It’s far more comfortable browsing this virtual phone, then rather use a phone in real life obviously, since the game grants resolutions up to your own. Videos and pictures follow the expected quality and it’s an authentic experience as far as design goes.

Indie games featuring live-action performances with quality are rare. Most of the times the studio goes to an alternative or stylized acting. [b]SIMULACRA[/b] though, doesn’t need any of those tricks, and [url=www.instagram.com/wendyvanhoren/]Wendy Van Horen[/url] plays Anna surprisingly well. Some may claim it’s an amateurish act, but remember, this is Anna’s life, a young person sharing vlogs about her personal life experiences. Wendy definitely brings the character alive, adding a natural and realistic touch.

[b]SIMULACRA[/b] dwells between our presence in the real world, versus our digital personas. I personally think it’s a really good concept and it’s well depict. Doesn’t become far-fetched, even when dealing with the supernatural. It’s a horror experience, but more towards what social media means to us, and how scary it can become. Very entertaining and for the simple price of $3,99 it’s impossible to avoid recommending this one.

review_text_raw:
My first experience with the found phone game genre was disappointing. I found [I]Replica[/I] to be an undercooked, preachy, borderline sciolistic game that is best not played. My excitement for this genre was quashed quickly, but I remembered that I still have [I]SIMULACRA[/I] in my backlog of games. Because of that, I decided to give found phone games another try.

Coincidentally, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] was partly inspired by [I]Replica[/I] (as seen by the titles), and partly by [I]Her Story[/I], one of my favourite games of all time. I loved [I]Her Story[/I] for its intriguing narrative and presentation, so I had some hope for [I]SIMULACRA[/I]. Thankfully, after my disheartening first exposure to found phone games, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] did not disappoint.

[I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a mystery game, in which you find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna. By digging deep into her personal life chronicled by the contents of her phone and Internet activities, you uncover clues as to why Anna had gone missing. The puzzles in this game are fun, fair, and hardly difficult. Because of that, the game manages to present the story in a nice flow. It also helps that [I]SIMULACRA[/I] has a slick presentation, with a clean, Android-like user interface that controls well with mouse and keyboard. The in-game videos are pretty well done, too, but I did find the voice acting for one particular character to be laughable.

Despite [I]SIMULACRA[/I] being described or classified as a horror game, I did not find it scary.  Aside from a few instances, in which some players may find the game's version of a "jump scare" frightening, I considered this game to be more suspenseful. You can feel the plot thickening and tension building as the game progresses, with some subtle (but usually not so subtle) graphical and audio alterations making the game increasingly unnerving. The way [I]SIMULACRA[/I]'s story unfolds is almost Hitchcockian.

As much as I enjoyed the game narrative, I did find the ending slightly abrupt. It seemed like there is more story to tell, and perhaps the spin-off game, [I]SIMULACRA: Pipe Dreams[/I], may tie up some loose ends. Still, [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is a very enjoyable game, made even better if played in the dark with earphones on. The developers smartly included a "Begin+" mode that will unlock after the first playthrough. This mode allows you to replay the entire game with sped-up text, so you can retry certain scenarios without needing to sit through the slow, deliberate pace of the chat sessions. (It's also a time saver for achievement hunters.) [I]SIMULACRA[/I] gets an enthusiastic recommendation from me.

P.S.: I wrote this review after completing [I]Sara is Missing[/i] the predecessor of this game. [I]SIMULACRA[/I] shares many similarities with [I]S.I.M.[/I] (Coincidence? I think not!), and [I]SIMULACRA[/I] is clearly more refined in both story and game mechanics. Both games are worth playing, as they are both good ambassadors for the found phone game genre.

[h1]Final Verdict: Buy! Spoiler-Free Review.[/h1]

This game took me about 3.5 hours to complete on my first playthrough (there are alternate endings available). I tried to read every bit of text and watch every video / photo involved. This game does disappoint as a horror game, but as a mystery thriller, it is excellent. 

This is not a mixed or alternate reality game where you search the web for answers or give your e-mail. The experience is pretty linear, although you can make different choices, the experience goes pretty much through the same set of main events (except for the endings which can vary). You will be looking through videos, photos, Jabbr (facebook), Spark (Tinder), the web (in-game only browser), phone numbers, and e-mails. You simply have to find the relevant information to unlock passcodes or find connections to progress the story. 

You will also have dialogue choices. Some of those choices can have an impact on the story, for example, having more trust with that person and thus giving you a different ending. The story starts out very strong when it is a mystery about what happened to the missing woman, Anna. Even the creepy stuff is exciting at first when you see the distorted videos and the atmosphere leaves things to the imagination. The dialogue between characters is well-written. 

Unfortunately, when you find out the mystery then the horror elements become more silly than scary. I actually just started to troll everybody, trying to get the worst possible ending. There was some real tension at the start and middle of this game, but towards the end, I really didn't feel any connection to any of the characters or "the danger" involved.

That's a shame because this is a very polished experience. The actors all did a nice job overall (sure some of the acting could have been better, but it's better than what is in most games). The mystery sequences where you're sleuthing and trying to find the truth all work extremely well. It's just too bad it ends in a whimper instead of a bang.

[b]Rate 7/10. I still recommend this. With a better ending(s), this could have been something very special. Good overall, but should have been great![/b]

review_text_raw:
Simulacra is an interesting horror game where the events unfold through a phone screen.

Story:

You play as an unnamed man/woman. We find a phone that belongs to a woman named Anna, we find a message of her begging for help and well we launch into an investigation to figure out how to save her.

The story in Simulacra is quite intriguing and all the research you do to figure out what happened to Anna and all the people around her, is quite interesting, because you go through many sites, reading articles and text messages, most of it having some decent writing behind it.

Graphics:

Well the only graphics in this is your phone. The phone has it's own OS named Iris and it's styled after an android phone. It looks quite convincing. You definitely know what each app represents so the art team definitely nailed the look of a smart phone.

Audio:

The acting is pretty sub-par, the actress that plays Anna is the only one that is semi-decent, but everyone else does a pretty mediocre job. However where the game shines the most is in it's audio design. The noises you hear around you when you browse the phone send a shiver down your spine. It could be something simple, like a small whisper to a creepy silent laugh. 

Gameplay:

Simulacra is mostly a puzzle solving game, where you have goals and you have to figure out how solve and these puzzles have a pretty decent design. A liked quite a few of the puzzles and how fresh they felt.

These puzzles range from pretty simple to sometimes head scratching. But it never felt cryptic and actually quite a few of the puzzles required a really logical solution and it felt like it would be something I would do in real life. 

You can do a bunch of research by reading articles, reading text messages so there's a lot of stuff to do in the phone. Also not to mention there's multiple choices throughout the story and multiple endings for you to achieve. 

Verdict:

Simulacra is a pretty unique horror game and it's story is pretty intriguing. With multiple endings and a really interesting plot I loved my time with this game and honestly I suggest giving it a shot at full price.

Pros:
+ Story is pretty intriguing
+ Nails the look of a smartphone perfectly
+ Multiple choices lead to different outcomes and endings
+ Great puzzles

Cons:
- Acting is not good whatsoever 

Final Rating:
8.5/10

review_text_raw:
[This review made after getting two bad endings out of 5 possible endings]

I like this game and I would recommend it, first and foremost, to players that are interested in STORY or, at least, world 
building. The game is not difficult: picture puzzles, word arranging, and some light fact searching comprise the bulk of the challenges. The meat of the game is in the dialogue choices, and this is where the replayability come from. You don't really get locked out of most options when taking/talking different ways, so you can express your moral flexibility without fearing that you'll reach a dead-end. As for content, they did a decent job of fleshing out with stuff that makes it feel like a "lived with" phone. The game does a good job of simulating smartphone usage with the apps, pics and their poses, vids, and social media content. A nice touch, is that there is a checklist of tasks that would help the truly clueless and serve as a guide for those looking for certain keystone events to play around with on subsequent playthroughs. This checklist is out of the way though for those who don't want hints on what to do next.


On the negative side, some of the voice acting, for me, was off if not "unsuitable". The delivery of the voice only lines truly felt and sounded "rehearsed". The VOs not sounding natural kind of sticks out like a sore thumb amid the aptness of the pictures and videos to a phone setting. The worst offender of this, sorry to say to the voice actor, is the Greg character. Truly, to me, it sounded like he was voicing a cartoon character instead of making a call, and it kind of took me out of the general mood of the game.

I think, the ending, will be pretty hit or miss for some people as well. I want to liken how the ending progresses to one of the scenes in a movie, but that would probably spoil it a bit. It's just that most people that saw it back then went "Wait what was that again?" Don't get me wrong, I'm fine with the endings I got (two bad endings), but the way to the climax was tedious, especially since I don't know if there is a message skip button for when you are doing a replay and you know what is going to be said. A note on the endings I got, it seems like you get locked to a set of outcomes after some threshold. I know my choices at the end didn't end up changing any of my final options. 

All in all, a decent casual horror sim game with some replayability, a fleshed out setting, hit or miss voice acting, and an endgame sequence (not ending, the stuff leading up to the ending) that'll make you go "excuse you? whowherewhenhowwhywhatnow?". 

For now, at full price, it would depend on your affinity for games like these to buy it for around a 5 hour single playthrough (worth it if you go with the $1 per hour of gameplay mindset). It is a decent recommend to buy if it ever has a sale at some point though.

Picture this: you find a girl's phone, and her name is Anna. But here's the catch - she's missing, and you're the one holding her phone with all its personal information. Creepy, right?

The story revolves around investigating Anna's disappearance, and as you interact with her friends and family through text messages and phone conversations, the tension keeps building up. The drama feels real, and the game's decision-based mechanics force you to make choices that affect the outcome. The best part is, it's not just a mystery unraveling over time; your main goal is clear - find Anna. But beware, Simulacra is not just about jumpscares; it plays with your senses more subtly, with eerie audio effects that might even make you question reality outside the game.

Though the game is quite engaging, it's not without its flaws. The voice acting feels a bit awkward and scripted, and some audio elements seem unnecessary, primarily existing for the sake of providing a jumpscare. But hey, the recorded videos are well done, especially Anna's personal vlogs.

Playing this game on PC might not be as immersive as on a mobile phone but it holds its merit reguardless. Still, they could've allowed portrait mode like in Downwell to make it even better.

All in all, Simulacra is a decent horror title that excels in subtle horror and decision-based gameplay. Simulacra is a simulated mobile phone method of delivering a horror game. It is based on the disappearance of a young woman named Anna, and the protagonist (you) has discovered her phone on their doorstep. From there, you delve into the secrets of her phone to find all the information you can, and try to locate--and subsequently save--Anna.

From a mechanical perspective, the game is pretty solid. There's no skeleton or standard out there for "Phone application based horror", making Simulacra a rather noteworthy pioneer and sequel to the developer's predecessor. Applications are sound, mimicking their real-life counterparts exceptionally well. The interface is smooth, and the methods for accessing the different pools of data prove acceptable. My only real complaint is, while the "data restoration" mechanic was easy enough to use, it felt ultimately meaningless and proved only to be a minor time sink. It was an interesting concept, but executed poorly. Perhaps, in later editions, the method for restoring and recovering data might make a more central point in the story.

However, in a game like this, the story is what really holds the fiber and and strength of a game. Hoo boy, does Simulacra tell you a story. The deeper you delve, the closer you get, the more stressful the game will become. Information will consistently surprise the player, and force them to make intensely difficult decisions. While they do have some effect on the ending of the game, the limitation to four significant endings does, to say the least, cause some level of dissonance between decision making and results.

Overall, for five dollars, it was a surprisingly binge-worthy experience.
